title: Product Measures and the Fubini Tonelli Theorems

items.title: Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces
The product $\sigma$-algebra and its finite iterates
Finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles form an algebra generating the product $\sigma$-algebra
items.strategy: Use the rectangle intersection and complement formulas to show that finite unions of measurable rectangles form an algebra. Then disjointify any finite union by the usual refinement into intersection cells, and note that adjoining finite unions does not change the generated $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The product measure can also be constructed from the rectangle algebra by Caratheodory extension
Sections E_x, E^y, f_x, and f^y on a product
Every section of a product-measurable set is measurable
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal M$ be the class of subsets of $X \times Y$ whose horizontal and vertical sections are measurable. Rectangle sections are measurable, and the section formulas commute with complements and countable unions. Thus $\mathcal M$ is a $\sigma$-algebra containing the measurable rectangles, so it contains the whole product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: Every section of a product-measurable function is measurable
items.strategy: Test measurability against a generating family of Borel subsets of the codomain. The preimage of each such generator under a fixed section is the corresponding section of a product-measurable subset of $X \times Y$, so the previous theorem applies.

items.title: FALSE: if every horizontal and vertical section is measurable, then the set is product-measurable
items.strategy: Use a classical set in $[0,1]^2$ whose horizontal sections are countable and whose vertical sections are cocountable, while the set itself is not measurable in the product $\sigma$-algebra. The witness shows that sectionwise measurability is genuinely weaker than joint measurability.

items.title: For $\sigma$-finite measures, the section-measure functions are measurable
items.strategy: First handle indicator functions of measurable rectangles, then finite disjoint unions of rectangles, and then the monotone class generated by that algebra. Sigma-finiteness is used to exhaust the factors by finite-measure pieces so that the monotone class argument starts from finite values.

items.title: For $\sigma$-finite measures, the two section-measure integrals of a measurable set agree
items.strategy: Verify the equality on measurable rectangles, extend it to finite disjoint unions by additivity, and then pass to the monotone class of measurable sets for which the equality holds. Monotone convergence upgrades the equality from indicators to arbitrary increasing unions inside the exhaustion by finite-measure rectangles.

items.title: The product measure of two $\sigma$-finite measure spaces
For $\sigma$-finite factors, the product measure exists, has the rectangle formula, is $\sigma$-finite, and is unique
items.strategy: Define $(\mu \times \nu)(E)$ by the common value of the two section-measure integrals. Indicator functions on rectangles give the rectangle formula, additivity on measurable unions gives the measure axioms, and exhaustions by finite-measure sets make the product $\sigma$-finite. Uniqueness follows from the published theorem for measures agreeing on a $\sigma$-finite generating $\pi$-system.

items.title: FALSE: the rectangle formula determines a unique product measure without any $\sigma$-finiteness hypothesis
items.strategy: Use Lebesgue measure on one copy of $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other. The usual primitive product and the locally determined product agree on measurable rectangles but assign different values to the diagonal, so uniqueness fails exactly when the $\sigma$-finite hypothesis is removed.

items.title: Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions on a $\sigma$-finite product
items.strategy: Start from indicators of measurable sets, where the statement is the section-measure theorem. Extend to nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and then to arbitrary nonnegative measurable functions by increasing simple approximation and monotone convergence.

items.title: FALSE: Tonelli's theorem still holds without any $\sigma$-finiteness hypothesis
items.strategy: Take Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other factor, and test Tonelli on the indicator of the diagonal. One iterated integral is $1$ while the other is $0$, so the Tonelli equality fails once the counting-measure factor is not $\sigma$-finite.

items.title: Fubini's theorem for $L^1$ functions on a $\sigma$-finite product
items.strategy: Apply Tonelli to $|f|$ to obtain almost-everywhere integrability of the sections and integrability of the section-integral functions. Then decompose $f$ into real and imaginary, or positive and negative, parts and use linearity to recover the signed statement.

items.title: To use Fubini safely, first use Tonelli on $|f|$
The completed product measure
Tonelli and Fubini for the completed product, with only almost-everywhere section measurability
items.strategy: Represent a completed-product measurable function by a base measurable representative that agrees almost everywhere. Apply the uncompleted theorem to that representative, then transport the conclusion back across almost-everywhere equality. The pointwise section statements weaken to almost-everywhere statements because the null exceptional set can meet some sections completely.

items.title: FALSE: every section of a completed-product measurable function is measurable
items.strategy: Take the indicator of a subset of a product-null line whose exceptional section is a nonmeasurable set. The function is measurable for the completion because it is supported on a null set, but the offending section is not measurable for the original factor measure.

items.title: The Borel product of $\mathbb R^m$ and $\mathbb R^n$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$
items.strategy: Use the identification $\mathbb R^{m+n} = \mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n$. Rational boxes generate the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra, so one inclusion is immediate. For the converse, second countability lets every open subset of the product be a countable union of open rectangles, placing every open set in the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The equality B(X) tensor B(Y) = B(X x Y) needs second countability
On Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$, the product $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ agrees with $\lambda_{m+n}$
items.strategy: Transfer the product measure to the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra through the previous identification. Both measures are Borel, $\sigma$-finite, and translation invariant, and they agree on rational half-open boxes because both compute their value as the product of side lengths. Uniqueness of normalized translation-invariant Borel measure on Euclidean space then forces equality.

items.title: The Euclidean Lebesgue measure is the completion of the product of the factor Lebesgue measures
items.strategy: The product measure agrees with $\lambda_{m+n}$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, while the published Euclidean result identifies the full Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra as the completion of that Borel measure. Therefore the completion of $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ on the product $\sigma$-algebra is exactly $\lambda_{m+n}$.

items.title: FALSE: the product of two complete measure spaces is complete
items.strategy: Take the Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra on each factor and place a nonmeasurable subset on a null vertical line. The ambient line is product-null, but the subset itself is not in the product $\sigma$-algebra because one of its sections is nonmeasurable.

items.title: FALSE: $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m) \otimes \mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ already equals $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$
items.strategy: Use the same null-line witness as for incompleteness. It is Lebesgue measurable in the product Euclidean space because it lies inside a null set, but it is not in the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebras.

items.title: The region under a nonnegative measurable function is product-measurable and has measure equal to the integral
items.strategy: Express the subgraph as the indicator domain of the section lengths $t \mapsto \mathbf 1_{[0,f(x))}(t)$. Measurability of the region is equivalent to measurability of $f$, and Tonelli applied to the indicator function computes the product measure as the integral of the section lengths.

items.title: The graph of a measurable function $\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ is Lebesgue null
items.strategy: The graph is measurable as the intersection of the two subgraphs of $f$ and of $-f$. For each base point its vertical section is a singleton or empty, hence one-dimensional Lebesgue null. Tonelli applied to the graph indicator then gives total measure zero.

items.title: The distribution function of absolute value
For $0 < p < \infty$, the layer-cake formula computes $\int |f|^p$ from the distribution function
items.strategy: Apply the region-under-the-graph theorem to the nonnegative measurable function $|f|^p$, then rewrite its subgraph by the change of variable $t = s^p$. One integration-by-parts step in the one-variable parameter yields the formula with the factor $p s^{p-1}$.

items.title: The Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ induced by polar decomposition
Polar coordinates decompose Lebesgue measure into $r^{n-1} \, dr \, d\sigma$
items.strategy: Define the candidate sphere measure by the unit-ball shell formula and verify the product identity first on radial rectangles $(a,b] \times E$. Uniqueness on the product Borel $\sigma$-algebra then identifies the pushed-forward measure under $(r,\omega) \mapsto r\omega$, and Tonelli upgrades the set identity to the integral formula.

items.title: The polar formula recovers the published $n$-ball volumes and Gaussian constants
A $C^1$ diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue null sets to Lebesgue null sets
items.strategy: Cover the null set by a Borel null superset, decompose that superset into compact pieces, and apply the linearized change-of-variables estimate on each compact set. The image of each null compact is null, and countable subadditivity finishes.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue measurable sets to Lebesgue measurable sets
items.strategy: Write a Lebesgue measurable set as a Borel set plus a null modification. Continuous images of Borel sets remain Borel, and the previous lemma handles the null correction on both the set and its complement.

items.title: The published Riemann change-of-variables theorem already gives the Lebesgue formula for continuous compactly supported integrands
items.strategy: Choose a compact Jordan neighborhood containing the support and apply the published change-of-variables theorem there. Jordan and Lebesgue integration agree on compact Jordan sets, so the Riemann formula is already the Lebesgue formula for this class of integrands.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for nonnegative Lebesgue measurable functions
items.strategy: Start from continuous compactly supported functions, extend to open sets by monotone convergence along compact exhaustions, pass from Borel sets to Lebesgue measurable sets by Borel approximation and null-set invariance, and then approximate an arbitrary nonnegative measurable function from below by simple functions.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for $L^1$ functions
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative theorem to the positive and negative parts, or equivalently to the real and imaginary parts, and then recombine by linearity once Tonelli has shown that the transformed absolute value is integrable.

items.title: Finite product measures are the base case for later countable-product constructions

title: Product Measures and the Fubini Tonelli Theorems — Examples

items.title: Tonelli and the plane polar formula give $\int_{\mathbb R} e^{-x^2} \, dx = \sqrt{\pi}$
items.strategy: Square the one-dimensional Gaussian integral formally, identify the square with the product integral of $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$, use Tonelli to justify the product, and then import the published plane polar computation.

items.title: Tonelli and the geometric series compute $\int_0^1 \! \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-xy} \, dx \, dy = \pi^2/6$
items.strategy: Expand $(1-xy)^{-1}$ into its nonnegative geometric series on the unit square, apply Tonelli termwise, and identify the resulting double series with $\sum_{n \ge 1} n^{-2}$.

items.title: The region under $x \mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$ has measure $1/3$
items.strategy: Apply the region-under-the-graph theorem to $f(x)=x^2$, and then evaluate the resulting one-variable integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

items.title: Cavalieri computes the area of the unit disc from its sections
items.strategy: Write the disc indicator as a nonnegative measurable function on $[-1,1] \times \mathbb R$, identify each vertical section length as $2\sqrt{1-x^2}$, and use Tonelli to recover the area by a one-variable integral.

items.title: A set can have measurable horizontal and vertical sections and still fail to be product-measurable
items.strategy: Use a classical well-ordered subset of the square whose horizontal sections are countable and whose vertical sections are cocountable. Every section is measurable, but the set itself is not measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The diagonal under Lebesgue times counting measure shows that Tonelli needs $\sigma$-finiteness
items.strategy: Take $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure on one side and counting measure on the other, and test Tonelli on the indicator of the diagonal. The two iterated integrals are $1$ and $0$.

items.title: The function $(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ shows that Fubini's integrability hypothesis is not decorative
items.strategy: Integrate first in $y$ using the antiderivative $y/(x^2+y^2)$ to obtain $1/(1+x^2)$ and hence $\pi/4$, then swap the variables to obtain $-\pi/4$. The absolute value is not integrable near the origin.

items.title: Equal iterated integrals still do not imply product integrability
items.strategy: Place the previous counterexample and its coordinate-swapped copy on two disjoint squares. Their two discrepancies cancel, so the iterated integrals agree, but each square still carries a nonintegrable singularity and the total absolute integral diverges.

items.title: Without $\sigma$-finiteness, the rectangle formula need not determine a unique product measure
items.strategy: For Lebesgue measure on one copy of $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other, compare the primitive product measure with the locally determined section-sum product. They agree on measurable rectangles but give different values to the diagonal.

items.title: A nonmeasurable subset of a null line shows that the product of complete measures need not be complete
items.strategy: Inside $\mathbb R^2$, place a nonmeasurable subset on a null vertical line. The ambient line is product-null, but the subset fails the section test for membership in the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: A completed-product measurable set can have a nonmeasurable exceptional section
items.strategy: Use the same null-line subset as in the incompleteness example, but view its indicator as a function measurable for the completed product. The exceptional section at the supporting base point is exactly the chosen nonmeasurable set.
